:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Determine the vertical asymptotes of $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2-x-6}{x^3 - 3 x^2 + x - 3}.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}-x-6}{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+x-3} \\  & =\frac{(x+2)(x-3)}{{x}^{2}(x-3)+(x-3)} \\  & =\frac{(x+2)(x-3)}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-3)} \\  & =\frac{(x+2)\cancel{(x-3)}}{({x}^{2}+1)\cancel{(x-3)}} \\  & =\frac{x+2}{{x}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
x^2 + 1 = 0
$$

This equation does not have any real solutions because the discriminant $\mathcal D$ is negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(0{)}^{2}-4(1)(1) \\  & =0-4 \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has no vertical asymptotes.

:answer-field/choices.:answer/value: The function has no vertical asymptotes

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x+1}{{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+x+1} \\  & =\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}(x+1)+(x+1)} \\  & =\frac{x+1}{(x+1)({x}^{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{x+1}}{\cancel{(x+1)}({x}^{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
{x}^{2}+1=0
$$

This equation does not have any real solutions. Therefore, $f(x)$ does not have any vertical asymptotes.
